But Deere claims max engine power 437 kW (594 hp) and rated PTO power 249 kW (335 hp). 274.55 kW PTO = 368 hp PTO. The Case IH 2188 PTO max = 541.99 hp (404 kW). So the Case IH test shows much higher PTO power (404 kW) than the Deere test (274.55 kW). That's odd — these are rated as the same nominal class (540 hp engine). 

Explanation: the Deere test in the OECD abstract may be a de-rated test configuration (PTO-limited by the 1000-rpm PTO rating), or the OECD abstract reports a different test point. Deere's rated PTO power is 249 kW (335 hp) — the OECD "one hour test at maximum power" of 274.55 kW (368 hp PTO) is plausibly a PTO-limited max. Meanwhile Case IH's 541.99 hp PTO (404 kW) is at the engine's max power. Case IH rated PTO 473 hp (352.7 kW); the 2188 test max PTO 541.99 hp = 404 kW, above rated — that's the max-power 1-hour test.

Hmm, the numbers really aren't apples-to-apples on power level. The Deere PTO test tops out at 274.55 kW (368 hp) whereas Case IH PTO tops at 404 kW (542 hp). So a direct SFC comparison is somewhat compromised — but specific fuel consumption (g/kWh) is normalized, so it's a fair efficiency metric as long as both are measured the same way. However, the Deere's best SFC (230 g/kWh) occurred at max power (274.55 kW) and the Case IH's best was 0.355 lb/hp-hr = 231 g/kWh at its standard PTO speed. Let me convert:

Case IH 0.355 lb/hp-hr → g/kWh: 0.355 lb/hp-hr × 453.592 g/lb ÷ 0.7457 kWh/hp-hr = 161.0/0.7457 = 215.9 g/kWh. 
Let me redo: 0.355 lb/hp-hr = 0.355 × 453.592 g/hp-hr = 161.03 g/hp-hr. Per kWh: 161.03 / 0.7457 = 215.9 g/kWh.
And 0.359 → 162.84/0.7457 = 218.4 g/kWh.
And 0.381 → 172.82/0.7457 = 231.8 g/kWh.

So Case IH best: 215.9–218.4 g/kWh. Deere best: 230 g/kWh. Difference = (230-215.9)/230 = 6.1%. 

And Deere at standard PTO speed 236 g/kWh vs Case IH at its standard PTO speed 215.9 g/kWh → 8.5%.

Good, so the SFC advantage of the Case IH FPT 12.9L (SCR-only, no DPF) is ~5-8.5% on these OECD/Nebraska PTO tests.

BUT: important caveat — Deere's JD14 also eliminated the DPF (per Deere's own page), so this isn't a DPF-vs-SCR story anymore; it's likely a combustion/aftertreatment calibration difference. Also, the Deere test is on a *newer* engine (2023) with presumably tighter emissions. And crucially, fuel efficiency at the drawbar depends also on track/undercarriage efficiency and ballasting, where I have no head-to-head number.

Also note: Deere's max power test at 230 g/kWh is quite good, and Deere's rated-speed test at 250 g/kWh is poor. So Deere wants to run at high power/high rpm-drop. Case IH is more consistent (0.355-0.359 across the range).

**Drawbar efficiency comparison — the one drawbar data point I have:**
- Steiger 540 wheeled (2096): 441.44 hp drawbar, 26.6 gal/h → 16.59 hp-hr/gal, 2.9% slip
- 9RX 540 (2310 - single turbo, newer): drawbar fuel rate at 540 engine hp: 171.7–185.4 lb/h. If this is at max drawbar power... at 7.047 lb/gal (approx) → 24.4-26.3 gal/h. Hmm, but this is "drawbar operations (540 engine hp)" fuel rate range, which represents engine fuel at 540 engine hp during drawbar operations. Without the corresponding drawbar power, I can't compute hp-hr/gal.

Deere 9RX 540 (2252): drawbar ops fuel 174.8–189.4 lb/h → /7.047 = 24.8–26.9 gal/h at 540 engine hp.
Case IH 540 Quadtrac PTO at max power: 27.81 gal/h at 541.99 PTO hp.
So at ~540 hp, Deere burns ~24.8–26.9 gal/h in drawbar work; the Case IH PTO test at 542 hp burned 27.81 gal/h PTO. Not directly comparable (drawbar ops vs PTO), but roughly similar hourly burn at ~540 hp. This suggests the real drawbar fuel difference is smaller than the PTO SFC difference, OR that the Deere "540 engine hp" drawbar fuel rate range corresponds to less than 540 hp net.

Also the 9RX 540 OECD drawbar max power is 348.85 kW = 468 hp at 11.70 km/h, on a 26,564 kg unballasted machine. Interesting: Deere's drawbar max power 468 hp from a 540-rated-hp engine (87% drawbar/engine ratio) vs Case IH wheeled Steiger 540's 441.44 hp from 535 engine hp (82.5%). But those are different years/conditions.

Hmm wait, actually the Deere max drawbar power 348.85 kW = 467.9 hp at 11.70 km/h — and if that was at ~24.8-26.9 gal/h we'd get 17.4-18.9 hp-hr/gal. That's better than the Case IH wheeled 16.59. But I can't tie the fuel rate range to the max power point reliably. I'll present both with caveats.

Actually — the OECD abstract says maximum power 348.85 kW at 11.70 km/h. And the Nebraska 2252 says "Drawbar operations (540 engine hp) 174.8–189.4 lb/h". If max drawbar is 348.85 kW = 468 hp, then fuel at 189.4 lb/h = 26.9 gal/h → 468/26.9 = 17.4 hp-hr/gal. And at 174.8 lb/h = 24.8 gal/h → 18.9 hp-hr/gal. So ~17.4-18.9. Hmm, that would make the 9RX quite efficient at the drawbar — better than the 2017 Case IH wheeled 540 (16.59). But that's a wheeled Case IH vs tracked Deere, and different eras. Not a valid comparison. I'll present as suggestive only.

Let me be careful and just present: Deere 9RX 540 drawbar op fuel at 540 engine hp = 24.8–26.9 gal/h (174.8–189.4 lb/h ÷ 7.047 lb/gal). Case IH 540 Quadtrac max PTO test 27.81 gal/h at 542 hp. So hourly burn is similar; specific efficiency differs 5-8.5% on PTO tests.

**Now the 10-year cost model.** Let me build a framework with explicit numbers where I have them and placeholders where I don't.

Inputs I have:
- Case IH Steiger 540 Quadtrac 2015 list price: $514,789
- Case IH claim: up to $1,000/yr lower ownership+maintenance vs comparable Deere; 2.1% lower total operating cost ($0.0023/hp-hr); 685 h/yr and 75% power assumption; 600-hr oil change (Case IH) vs 450-hr (most competitors)
- Deere claim: JD14 with no DPF, HPCR, automatic valve lash, one aftertreatment canister → "boost fuel efficiency and lower operation and maintenance costs"

Let me compute a 10-year cost per hectare with a scenario.

Scenario: 685 h/yr, 75% power (~405 hp), 10 years = 6,850 h.
Fuel at ~20.5 gal/h (interpolating Case IH curve: at 417 hp 23.63 gal/h; at 75% of 542 hp = 406 hp → ~23.2 gal/h = 87.8 L/h). Actually at 417 hp the Case IH used 23.63 gal/h. At 406 hp ≈ 23.3 gal/h = 88.2 L/h.
10 years: 6,850 × 88.2 = 604,170 L. At $1.30/L = $785,421.
If the Deere burns 6% more: +36,250 L = +$47,125 over 10 years.

Output: 685 h/yr × 10 yr × ~7.5 ha/h = 51,375 ha worked over 10 years.
Fuel cost per hectare: $785,421 / 51,375 = $15.29/ha (Case IH).
If Deere 6% worse: $16.21/ha. Delta $0.92/ha.

Total cost per hectare: machine price + resale + fuel + maintenance + DEF + labor.
Price: assume $550,000-$900,000 purchase (2024-25). I only have the 2015 $514,789 figure. I'll use it as an anchor and note that current prices are materially higher but unrecovered.
Over 51,375 ha: $514,789 / 51,375 = $10.02/ha in capital. At $800,000 → $15.57/ha. Resale at 40-45% after 10 yr/6,850 h recovers some.

Let me build a simple table. I'll present capital, fuel, DEF, maintenance, and the delta.

DEF: Case IH 540 Quadtrac at max power uses 2.86 gal/h DEF (2017 test). Deere OECD abstract: 2.56 l/h at max power (one-hour test), 3.25 l/h at rated-speed max power, 2.55 l/h at standard PTO speed. So DEF rates are comparable: Case IH 2.86 gal/h = 10.8 L/h at 542 hp PTO; Deere 2.56 L/h at 274.55 kW (368 hp PTO). Normalize: Deere 2.56 L/h per 274.55 kW = 9.3 mL/kWh; at standard PTO speed 2.55 L/h per 272.43 kW = 9.4 mL/kWh. Case IH 2.86 gal/h = 10.83 L/h per 404.16 kW = 26.8 mL/kWh.

Whoa, that's a 3x difference in DEF consumption per kWh! Let me double-check the Case IH number: In Test 2188 PTO table, "D.E.F. Consumption Gal/hr" at max power = 2.86 gal/hr. And "Diesel Consumption" 27.81 gal/hr. So DEF is ~10% of diesel by volume. Hmm — that's very high for SCR. Typical DEF:diesel ratio is 2-5%. 10% is unusual... Actually, wait. Some Nebraska reports list DEF in gallons per hour and the ratio being ~10% would be extreme. Let me reconsider — maybe the column is lb/h. The header reads "Diesel D.E.F. / Consumption Consumption / Gal/hr lb/hp.hr Hp.hr/gal Gal/hr". Hmm, so "Gal/hr" for diesel, then "lb/hp.hr", "Hp.hr/gal", then "Gal/hr" for DEF? Let me re-read: "Power Crank Diesel D.E.F. / HP shaft Consumption Consumption / (kW) speed Gal/hr lb/hp.hr Hp.hr/gal Gal/hr". So Diesel Consumption is in Gal/hr, lb/hp.hr, and Hp.hr/gal; and D.E.F. Consumption is in Gal/hr. So yes DEF = 2.86 gal/h at max power where diesel = 27.81 gal/h. That's 10.3% — very high. Hmm, but the Case IH test 2188's varying power row shows "2.46, 2.09, 1.62, 1.12, 0.65" for the first rows... those scale with load. At 480 hp, DEF 2.46 gal/h; at 106 hp, 0.65 gal/h. Ratio at 480 hp: 2.46/26.21 = 9.4%. Consistent ~9-10%.

Hmm, that's really high for an SCR-only system. But maybe they were running a conservative DEF dosing calibration, or the units are actually lb/h. Actually — wait: 2.86 "gal/hr" of DEF at 542 hp... DEF is ~1.087 kg/L. 2.86 gal/h = 10.83 L/h = 11.77 kg/h. Diesel at 27.81 gal/h = 105.3 L/h = 88.7 kg/h. DEF:diesel mass = 13.3%. Still ~13%. Hmm, that's much higher than typical. Some early Tier 4B systems did run high. Actually, note the Case IH page claims SCR-only (no EGR), which typically means LOWER DEF use per unit of NOx because of higher engine-out NOx... no, higher engine-out NOx means MORE DEF. Yes! SCR-only/ no-EGR engines have higher engine-out NOx and therefore need more DEF. That's consistent. Whereas EGR-equipped engines have lower engine-out NOx and use less DEF.

But the Deere JD14 at 9.3 mL/kWh = 0.0093 L/kWh. Case IH at 26.8 mL/kWh. Ratio 2.9x. Hmm. Let me check the Deere: is the abstract's "reagent" column in l/h too? "Hourly and specific reagent consumption/ Agent réducteur: Consommation horaire, Spécifique | 2.56 l/h | 10.1 g/kWh". So 10.1 g/kWh of DEF. Case IH: 11.77 kg/h over 404.16 kW = 29.1 g/kWh. So Case IH uses ~2.9x more DEF per kWh.

Hmm. That's a notable finding — the Deere JD14 with (presumably) EGR uses ~1/3 the DEF. That partially offsets Case IH's diesel advantage. Let me quantify:
- Case IH diesel saved: 6% of ~88 L/h = 5.3 L/h. At $1.30/L = $6.89/h.
- Case IH extra DEF: 29.1 - 10.1 = 19.0 g/kWh × 404 kW... but that's at full power. Normalize to 75% power (300 kW): 19.0 g/kWh × 300 kW = 5.7 kg/h = 5.24 L/h of DEF. At ~$1.00/L DEF (bulk) = $5.24/h.
So the DEF penalty roughly cancels the diesel savings! That's a genuinely useful analytical finding. Net: near parity, maybe slight Deere edge or near-neutral.

Hmm, but I should be careful: the Deere's 10.1 g/kWh was measured at 274.55 kW max power PTO test; DEF dosing is not linear with load — it's highest at high load/temperature. At part load, DEF dosing drops proportionally less/more. This is a rough extrapolation. I'll present it with appropriate uncertainty.

Actually, let me use DEF-per-fuel ratio instead, which is more robust:
- Deere: 2.56 L/h DEF / 74.62 L/h diesel = 3.43%
- Deere at standard PTO: 2.55/76.30 = 3.34%
- Deere at rated speed max power: 3.25/70.51 = 4.61%
- Case IH at max power: 2.86/27.81 = 10.28%
- Case IH at rated engine speed: 2.46/26.21 = 9.39%
- Case IH at standard PTO speed: 2.70/27.20 = 9.93%

So the Case IH burns DEF at ~9.4-10.3% of diesel volume; the Deere at 3.3-4.6%. Ratio ~2.3-2.9x. Clearly the Deere JD14 uses substantially less DEF. That's an important, novel, and quantitatively defensible finding.

Wait — but I should double check whether the 2017 Case IH test (2188) is Tier 4B with SCR only. The Case IH marketing says patented SCR, no DPF. And tractor-info says SCR Tier 4. Yes. And Deere's JD14 has "eliminated the diesel particulate filter" too and uses SCR — but Deere also uses cooled

# Trust-Building Mechanisms Across Argentina, Brazil, and Colombia: A Design Research Report for Gig Platform Expansion

## 1. Headline Findings

1. **Do not deploy one trust stack.** The single most decision-relevant finding is that the trust–sales relationship for the same platform (Mercado Libre, operating in 18 countries) is *statistically inconsistent across nations* even though trust is the strongest predictor of sales, ahead of purchase intention and price (https://perfiles.ibero.mx/ws/portalfiles/portal/328710679/Correa_et_al_2022_.pdf). A ratings model validated in São Paulo is not validated in Bogotá.

2. **Peer trust is not the lever in Brazil that it is in the literature.** In a study of 942 Brazilian consumers using structural equation modelling, trust in the platform, the product, and the user community positively influenced intention to use shared services — but **trust in peers did not directly affect intention to use** (https://periodicos.uninove.br/remark/article/view/30973). Designs that front-load peer reviews over platform guarantees are optimising the wrong variable in the largest LatAm market.

3. **Interpersonal trust baselines differ by roughly an order of magnitude**, which changes what a rating badge is *for*. 2023 Latinobarómetro data: Argentina 28%, Colombia 17%, Brazil **4%** agree "one can trust most people"; regional average 16% (https://azenha.ai/bulldozer/dashboards/latinobarometro). The Brazil country file shows 3.9% trusting most people versus 95.0% saying "one can never be too careful" (https://www.latinobarometro.org/documents/LAT-2023/latinobarometro-2023-brazil-v1-0.pdf). Latinobarómetro's 2024 wave (19,214 face-to-face interviews, 17 countries) describes Latin America as the world's lowest-trust region at roughly 15% (https://www.latinobarometro.org/documents/latinobarometro-informe-2024.pdf).

4. **Payment instruments have diverged sharply, and this is the biggest single design fork.** Brazil is Pix-first (67% of adults within Pix's first year; ~64bn transactions in 2024, +53% YoY — https://stripe.com/in/resources/more/pix-replacing-cards-cash-brazil). Argentina is wallet-and-QR-first (75% of adults hold ≥1 digital wallet; 73% hold 2+; https://iabargentina.com.ar/descargas/pago2024-kantar.pdf). Colombia is still **cash-on-delivery-first** — COD is 12% of e-commerce payments, the highest in LatAm, versus 4% in Argentina and 2% in Chile (https://www.revistafactordeexito.com/posts/39476/colombia-ocupa-primera-posicion-en-pagos-contra-entrega-en-latam).

5. **The dispute-resolution *interface* that Brazilians actually expect is external and public, not in-app.** Reclame Aqui reports >25 million resolved complaints, 900,000+ registered companies, and 33 million+ monthly visits, with a rule that a company failing to answer at least 50% of complaints is automatically labelled "Não Recomendada" (https://www.reclameaqui.com.br/, https://manual.reclameaqui.com.br/reputacao-no-reclame-aqui). Brazilian courts have reinforced this: a TJMG IRDR held that a consumer's *interesse de agir* depends on proof of an attempted amicable settlement, expressly citing Reclame Aqui, Consumidor.gov.br, Procon and the Central Bank channel as valid means (https://www.jusbrasil.com.br/artigos/consumidorgovbr-reclame-aqui-procon-ou-banco-central-qual-a-melhor-via-para-resolver-seus-problemas/5365032188).

6. **Argentina's state-backed pre-litigation mediation layer was dismantled in 2025**, removing a channel users had been trained to use. COPREC (Ley 26.993) was dissolved by Decreto 55/2025, published 3 February 2025; in 2024 it resolved 28% of 108,762 incoming claims at a cost of roughly AR$650 million annually (https://tecorresponde.com.ar/donde-reclamar, https://www.cronista.com/economia-politica/cierre-clave-en-defensa-al-consumidor-alertan-que-se-generaran-mas-costos/).

---

## 2. Evidence Base and Its Limits

This report draws on: multilateral and central-bank primary data (ILO, IADB, BCRA, Banco de la República), platform developer documentation and help centres (Mercado Livre, Uber, iFood, Rappi), peer-reviewed and practitioner academic studies (Frontiers in Communication, ReMark, Latin American Business Review, FGV, Fairwork), and civil-society/consumer-protection sources (Reclame Aqui, Procon, SIC, COPREC).

**Three material limitations, stated plainly:**

- **No experimental evidence exists specifically on how prior trust-system experience affects adoption in Argentina, Colombia, or Brazil.** The trust-transfer literature is dominated by Chinese and US e-commerce samples. The Brazilian ReMark study (n=942) is the closest direct evidence for this task. Everything else is inference by analogy, and I flag it as such.
- **The trust-transfer effect sizes are directionally robust but population-specific.** The moderating role of institutional mechanisms was established on 294 Taobao buyers (https://exa.ai/library/publication/k1hfkbzzhxw) — a market with different baseline institutional trust. Do not port coefficients.
- **Trust metrics are survey-sensitive.** For Brazil, the 2022 cross-survey table reports 10.2% (Latinobarómetro) versus 9.2% (Integrated Values Survey) — https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/interpersonal-trust-measured-in-different-surveys — while the 2023 country file reports 3.9%. Absolute levels are uncertain; **rankings are stable and that is what should drive design.** In every source, Brazil ranks lowest of the three and Argentina ranks highest among them.

---

## 3. Market Context: Informality and the Trust Baseline

### 3.1 Informality

The ILO puts regional informal employment at **47.6% in mid-2024**, down marginally from 48% in 2023 and 48.8% in 2019; Argentina's rate is cited at **43.2%** (https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2025-02/PL%202024_english_ExecutiveSummary.pdf, https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Social-policies_Covid-19_Informal-employment_Argentina-report_2024-en.pdf). Critically for a platform entering these markets, the ILO notes that **Argentina, Brazil and Mexico were exceptions** to the pattern in which informality drove employment growth — implying that in these three markets, platform work is absorbing labour from a *pre-existing* informal pool rather than creating new informal work. A São Paulo analysis makes the same point: the "traditional" informal sector has held stable at roughly **38% of the economically active population** while gig work remains a fraction of it, and platform-mediated work is the most fiscally *visible* informal work in the city's history — the platform invoices, withholds, and processes payment through a reporting financial institution (https://headreports.com/posts/myth-vs-reality-are-delivery-apps-actually-responsible-for-the-rise-in/).

**Design implication:** these users are not inexperienced with informal commerce. They are highly experienced with *unmediated, cash-based, trust-by-reputation-and-relationship* transactions. Your platform's trust mechanisms are competing with, not replacing, a working system.

### 3.2 Worker financial fragility

The IADB/IPSOS 2024 study of **more than 13,000 Uber drivers** across Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Dominican Republic and Argentina found drivers predominantly male, middle-aged, often part-time, mostly self-identifying as independent workers — but the majority report being **in debt** and using platform earnings for essential household needs, with low, fragmented social-protection coverage (https://publications.iadb.org/en/driving-through-gig-economy-latin-america-uber-drivers-views-needs-risks-and-opportunities). This matters because any trust mechanism that *withholds* money from a driver (escrow, hold, penalty) is felt as a liquidity shock, not an abstract rating event.

### 3.3 The incumbent trust infrastructure is financial, not social

The strongest existing trust proxy in these markets is a *financial app*, and its adoption was driven by word of mouth, not by institutional endorsement. Nubank reached **107.2 million customers in Brazil — 62% of the adult population — and banked 31.5 million people for the first time, roughly 1 in 5 Brazilian adults**; it is the leading "main bank" in every Brazilian region, with the strongest penetration in the lowest-GDP-per-capita states (https://nu.com/media/2026/07/DataNubank-8_2026_Nubanks-presence-and-impact-across-Brazil.pdf). In Colombia, Nu reached 5 million customers (~15% of adults) and issued a first-ever credit card to nearly 1 million people, in a country where roughly 65% had no formal credit access (https://international.nubank.com.br/company/nu-colombia-turns-five-with-5-million-customers-and-reinforces-its-long-term-commitment-to-the-country/). Earlier reporting notes **80–90% of Nubank customers were acquired organically through word-of-mouth or unpaid referral** (https://nextbillion.substack.com/p/understanding-nubank).

**Design implication:** referral and social proof are the highest-yield trust channels in this region — higher than badges or seals. Nubank's own framing is that the barrier is not access but **trust** (https://mastercardcontentexchange.com/news/media/1q0hfryx/mcg-24054-nubank-financial-inclusion-whitepaper_final.pdf).

## 4. Mechanism 1 — Rating and Reputation Systems

### 4.1 What works: reputation as an economic instrument, not a social signal

Mercado Livre's seller reputation is the region's most battle-tested model, and its architecture is instructive. The public API exposes reputation as a composite of `level_id` (e.g. `5_green`), `power_seller_status` (`platinum`), 60-day **claims rate**, 60-day **delayed handling time**, and 60-day **cancellations**, alongside historic positive/neutral/negative rating shares (https://developers.mercadolibre.com.bo/en_us/news/sellers-reputation). Two features are worth copying and one is worth scrutinising:

- **Behavioural metrics outweigh sentiment.** Claims, delays and cancellations are objective operational data. This reduces dependence on subjective star ratings — valuable where review manipulation perception is high (see 4.3).
- **The metrics are explicitly "excluded"-adjusted.** The payload returns both a headline rate and an `excluded.real_rate`. Displayed reputation is therefore a *policy-managed* artefact, with certain transactions removed before the score is shown.
- **Scrutinise the divergence.** The same API example returns `"level_id": "5_green"` and `"power_seller_status": "platinum"` alongside `"real_level": "red"`. A user sees green; the underlying classification is red. In a low-trust market, any leak or perception of this gap is a trust liability with outsized consequences.

### 4.2 Where it breaks: opacity and risk privatisation

Research on Mercado Libre third-party sellers in Chile documents that the platform **partially formalises informal commerce** — traceable payments, logistics, standardised transactions — while introducing *new* instabilities related to algorithmic visibility, reputation systems and changing participation rules. Sellers responded by **avoiding complaints at all costs**, responding immediately, and treating reputation-building as a form of entrepreneurship. The authors describe this as privatisation of risk onto individuals (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/29768624251414542).

An FGV master's thesis on mutual reputation among **Uber drivers in Brazil** found provider profiles with **different initial trust requirements**, and identified "the strong interference that intermediaries can exert on the usage of the reputation system by creating forms of provider's oppression," plus evidence of "sociomaterial bricolage" — providers inventing their own workarounds around the official rating system (https://pesquisa-eaesp.fgv.br/teses-dissertacoes/como-o-sistema-de-reputacao-baseado-em-avaliacao-mutua-e-utilizado-por). Fairwork Argentina reaches a consistent conclusion: worker autonomy "is frequently constrained by rankings, performance metrics, economic incentives, and digital reputation systems" (https://fair.work/en/fw/blog/platform-work-and-labour-reform-a-preview-of-the-future-of-work-in-argentina/).

### 4.3 Review authenticity is the primary trust risk in the rating layer

A study of 326 Mercado Libre Colombia buyers using confirmatory factor analysis and PLS-SEM found that **perceived fake reviews negatively affect trust in rating systems**, while **high-quality reviews positively influence all trust forms**; trust in the marketplace and in the rating system directly impact customer experience, with trust in the rating system **mediating** the relationship between fake-review perception and customer experience (https://public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1460321/pdf).

A separate Brazilian study of 470 respondents found customer-generated evaluation, perceived price, product delivery and information quality are the seller attributes that drive trust and repurchase intention in e-marketplaces (https://www.scielo.br/j/ram/a/PmSzKJZCBGnZ7xS45kDFDqc/?lang=). A further Brazilian analysis of 309 respondents confirmed that third-party seller reputation **negatively affects perceived risk and positively affects trust** in both the seller and the intermediary, with trust in the intermediary in turn reducing perceived risk and raising purchase intention (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10978526.2021.1893182).

**Caveat on credibility of the seal ecosystem:** an ANOVA study of 90 Brazilian e-commerce firms holding trust seals from eBIT and Reclame Aqui found **no coherence between Brazilian reputation systems**, reinforcing the presence of other predictive variables (https://www.redalyc.org/journal/840/84043515006/html/). Independent third-party seals are weaker signals than platform-native behavioural metrics.

### 4.4 Country-relevant rating design

| | Argentina | Brazil | Colombia |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline interpersonal trust (2023) | 28% | 4% | 17% |
| What the rating badge is doing | Confirms an existing disposition to trust | **Substitutes for absent interpersonal trust** | Supplement a moderate baseline |
| Priority design | Efficiency + dispute fairness; avoid ritualistic verification | Maximum verification credibility; anti-fraud visible; platform-guarantee over peer-opinion | Bridge digital/analogue; COD-native verification |

## 5. Mechanism 2 — Identity Verification Requirements

### 5.1 The identity infrastructure is genuinely asymmetric

A comparative technical assessment scores the three markets meaningfully differently (https://shuftipro.com/resources/whitepapers-reports/docless-identity-verification-latin-america/):

| Market | Identifier / registry | Government ID-validation service | National digital ID maturity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brazil | CPF (Receita Federal / CIN) | **Serpro Datavalid**, biographic + biometric | **gov.br — mature, 160M+ accounts, biometric gold tier** |
| Argentina | DNI (RENAPER / SIBIOS) | RENAPER SID, data, fingerprint and facial validation | DNI in Mi Argentina — **narrower** |
| Colombia | Cédula (RNEC base) | RNEC biometric service, authorised public and private entities | Autenticación Digital Ciudadana — **maturing** |

That same source notes that active verification — where the applicant authenticates with a national digital credential the issuer confirms in real time — is "genuinely strong in Brazil and Chile, real but narrower in Peru and **Argentina**, and still immature in Mexico."

### 5.2 Why a single KYC flow will fail

A LATAM KYC reference guide identifies the structural problem precisely: there is **no cross-border registry, no federated identity layer, no eIDAS equivalent**. CPF has a checksum digit; **Argentina's DNI does not**; CURP encodes birth date and gender in the string itself. A user moving from Bogotá to Buenos Aires starts from zero, and "every KYC stack you build has to handle at least one ID schema per country" (https://blog.gu1.ai/en/kyc-latam-complete-guide/). Validators confirm the checksum asymmetry: CPF (Mod-11), CUIL/CUIT (Mod-11) are algorithmically verifiable, whereas **DNI and Colombian Cédula are format-only** (https://rapidapi.com/sergiocalvog/api/latam-id-validator1, https://github.com/sergiocalvog/latam-id-validator/blob/refs/heads/main/README.md).

Regulatory fragmentation compounds this: BCB and COAF in Brazil, UIF and CNV in Argentina, UIAF in Colombia — "three SAR formats to three different FIUs on three different timelines" (https://blog.gu1.ai/en/kyc-latam-complete-guide/).

Brazil adds a further document-fragmentation problem relevant to visual verification: the RG is issued by each of Brazil's **26 states with different formats and security features**, which is why CPF-based validation against Receita Federal plus biometrics is preferred over document-image inspection (https://www.deepidv.com/media/smarthub/kyc-igaming-latin-america-brazil-colombia).

### 5.3 The onboarding-friction tradeoff is explicit and documented

Cross-border gig KYC guidance states the failure mode directly: "**Um KYC excessivamente complexo pode levar a altas taxas de abandono e impactar o crescimento da plataforma**" — excessively complex KYC leads to high abandonment and damages growth (https://didit.me/pt-BR/blog/composing-kyc-for-the-cross-border-gig-economy/). Automation is the mitigation: instant validation via national-registry integration moves onboarding from days to seconds and "dramatically improves conversion rates" (https://didit.me/pt-BR/blog/integrating-national-registries-neobank-onboarding-latam/).

**The counterexample worth noting on the sell side:** Mercado Livre requires only **CPF to start selling** — no CNPJ — and credits proceeds to a Mercado Pago account (https://www.mercadopago.com.br/blog/vender-mercado-livre-ecossistema-mercado-pago). That is the low-friction benchmark for supply-side onboarding in Brazil. Full KYB (with biometric liveness, UBO recursion, COAF and sanctions screening, 10-year evidence retention) is reserved for formal entities under Circular BACEN 3.978/2020 (https://dinheirodaminhaempresa.com/vender-e-receber/kyc-kyb-merchants/).

### 5.4 Platform practice: recurring, not one-time, verification

Identity verification in gig work is a *recurring* interface, and both major Brazilian platforms implement it as such:

- **Uber** requires delivery partners to complete identity verification **every 14 days**; failing to verify means the account cannot go online. Verification uses facial comparison via Microsoft as service provider, producing a **biometric faceprint**; flagged photos go to **human review by three identity-verification specialists**, with access lost if at least two fail the match (https://help.uber.com/pt-BR/driving-and-delivering/article/identity-verification-checks, https://help.uber.com/driving-and-delivering/article/how-does-uber-verify-my-photo).
- **iFood** applies facial recognition at specific trigger points: **new device access, profile data changes, and courier-initiated security requests** — comparing a selfie-derived "template facial" against the account record (https://institucional.ifood.com.br/entregadores/tira-teima-como-o-ifood-cadastra-e-verifica-os-entregadores/).

**Failure is not hypothetical, and it is legally consequential.** A Brazilian labour court (22ª Vara do Trabalho de Brasília) ordered iFood to pay **R$60,000 in moral damages** to courier Tiago Alves after the facial recognition system stopped recognising him — his defence argued a hairstyle change triggered the failure, and the case was framed as a "racist failure." The support team reportedly sent him photos of the supposed impostor that were photos of himself. iFood denied any racial analysis and appealed (https://g1.globo.com/df/distrito-federal/noticia/2025/06/30/justica-condena-ifood-a-indenizar-entregador-do-df-por-danos-morais-apos-falha-racista-em-reconhecimento-facial-entenda.ghtml).

This is corroborated at volume on public complaint channels: couriers report repeated facial-recognition failures triggering 7-day blocks after a year of clean work, with the complaint stating "**NÃO EXISTE nenhum canal entre entregador e Aplicativo Ifood para solucionar o problema**" (https://www.reclameaqui.com.br/ifood/bloqueio-de-entregador-ifood-devido-a-falha-no-reconhecimento-facial-e-aus_g33JCmiN6NXWFzxN/).

**Design implication:** verification is your highest-volatility trust surface. Build the *failure path* first — a human channel, a documented evidence-submission flow, an explicit SLA — because in a market where 95% of Brazilians say "one can never be too careful" (Latinobarómetro 2023), a false-positive rejection is read as betrayal, not error.

## 6. Mechanism 3 — Payment Escrow and Settlement

### 6.1 Reputation-conditioned escrow is the region's proven design

Mercado Pago is the native processor for Mercado Livre; every purchase — credit card, debit, **Pix, or boleto** — routes through it automatically, with no external integration required. Fund release timing is explicitly **a function of reputation**:

| Seller profile | Fund release |
|---|---|
| Good reputation + uses Mercado Envios | **2 days** after delivery confirmation |
| Still building history, or self-shipping | **up to 28 days** |
| MercadoLíderes | **up to 11 days** after buyer receipt, or **immediately** if buyer confirms first |

*(https://www.mercadopago.com.br/blog/vender-mercado-livre-ecossistema-mercado-pago)*

**Quantitative work:** the spread between the strongest and weakest release terms is **28 ÷ 2 = 14×**. Reputation here is not a cosmetic badge — it is directly equivalent to working capital. A Brazilian guide confirms the default logic: the sale value is held in Mercado Pago until delivery confirmation and released automatically after 7 days absent a problem (https://blog.bling.com.br/mercado-envios-o-que-e-como-funciona/).

Buyer-side escrow ("Compra Garantida") carries conditions that are themselves a UX contract: purchase on Mercado Livre, payment via Mercado Pago, returns only if received via Mercado Envios, active account, claim filed from the buyer account within applicable deadlines, and — notably — the buyer must **abstain from filing a chargeback with the card issuer** during or after the claim (https://www.reclameaqui.com.br/empresa/mercado-pago/conteudos/).

Seller protection against chargeback requires complete registration, **at least 10 completed sales**, payment for a tangible good, response within deadlines, and documentation including Nota Fiscal and delivery proof (https://www.mercadopago.com.br/blog/prevencao-fraudes-dia-das-maes). The 10-sale threshold is precisely the barrier a new informal seller has not cleared — an onboarding cliff worth designing around explicitly.

### 6.2 Brazil: Pix collapsed the payment-trust problem

Pix launched November 2020 with mandatory participation by large banks and fintechs, delivering national coverage on day one; it reached **67% of Brazilian adults within its first year** and **140 million Brazilians within two years**, and processed **~64 billion transactions in 2024 (+53% YoY)**, becoming the most-used payment method ahead of credit and debit cards (https://stripe.com/in/resources/more/pix-replacing-cards-cash-brazil).

**Derived figure, with assumptions stated:** if Brazil's adult population is approximately 173 million (inferred from Nubank's 107.2M customers = 62% of adults, per https://nu.com/media/2026/07/DataNubank-8_2026_Nubanks-presence-and-impact-across-Brazil.pdf), then 64bn ÷ 173M ≈ **370 Pix transactions per adult per year, or roughly 31 per adult per month.** This is a derivation, not a published statistic, and depends on the adult-population estimate.

The financial-inclusion effect: one estimate credits Pix with bringing **more than 70 million Brazilians their first bank account** (https://wfintechs.substack.com/p/108-credit-in-the-gig-economy-how). The IADB finds that a one-standard-deviation increase in pre-Pix mobile penetration produced a **1.2% wage increase in cash-intensive sectors** relative to non-cash-intensive sectors, concentrated among less-educated workers and reducing the college wage premium by about 1 percentage point (https://publications.iadb.org/en/financial-technologies-labor-markets-and-wage-inequality-evidence-instant-payment-systems).

Adoption is near-saturated among small business: a survey of **1,151 micro- and small-enterprise owners in Espírito Santo** found **97% use Pix**, with Pix transactions accounting for **nearly 90% of all non-cash business revenues** — though the majority flow through *personal* rather than business accounts, limiting eligibility for business financial products (https://poverty-action.org/how-pix-powering-open-finance-brazil).

**Caveat:** Pix is not universally accessible to non-residents, who may lack the CPF or local account required; cash remains a functional fallback in some app flows (https://www.adapay.asia/blog/uber-99-and-rappi-in-brazil).

### 6.3 Argentina: wallets and interoperable QR, not escrow

BCRA data shows a decisive shift. In 2024, the adult population made on average **more than 28 electronic payments per month, up 45% versus 2023** — the series runs 13.1 → 19.5 → 28.3, and 19.5 × 1.451 ≈ 28.3, confirming the growth rate. Cash withdrawals held flat at roughly **2.7–2.8 per adult per month**, giving an electronic-to-cash-withdrawal ratio of roughly **10.5:1** (https://www.bcra.gob.ar/archivos/Pdfs/PublicacionesEstadisticas/Abr25-ENG-Informe-de-Inclusion-Financiera.pdf).

By value, September 2024 saw electronic means of payment represent **95.3% of total transactions (MPE + cash), with cash at 4.7%**. Instrument mix: push transfers **50.1%**, debit cards **20.9%**, credit cards **14.5%**, payments-with-transfer (PCT) **4.5%** — of which **92% initiated by QR** — and direct debits/DEBIN 4.3% (https://mde.com.ar/assets/docs/4Sistema_financiero_MPE_11-24.pdf). The same source shows **Mercado Pago alone holds 81% of CVU-account balances** among payment service providers, administering funds equivalent to roughly the 10th-largest financial entity by private-sector deposits.

Interoperable QR reached **62.6 million transactions in December 2024, +117.4% YoY**, with **67 interoperable digital wallets registered** with the BCRA (https://www.bcra.gob.ar/en/publicaciones/retail-payments-report-december-2024/). Consumer behaviour: **75% of Argentine adults hold at least one digital wallet** (matching debit-card possession), **73% hold two or more**, and **65% park money in electronic accounts to earn yield while keeping it liquid** (https://iabargentina.com.ar/descargas/pago2024-kantar.pdf).

**Design implication for Argentina:** escrow is less necessary as a *payment-safety* device because the QR/wallet rail already carries strong institutional trust and instant settlement. Yield on idle balances is a genuine adoption driver — an escrow that visibly *forfeits* yield is a competitive disadvantage against Mercado Pago.

### 6.4 Colombia: cash-on-delivery is the trust mechanism

Colombia leads Latin America in COD — **12% of e-commerce payments**, versus Peru 10%, Argentina 4%, Mexico 3%, Chile 2%. Among merchants offering it (25% of Envíame's client base), COD accounts for **more than 40% of their sales**; Bogotá concentrates **45%** of deliveries (https://www.revistafactordeexito.com/posts/39476/colombia-ocupa-primera-posicion-en-pagos-contra-entrega-en-latam). The stated mechanism is unambiguous: COD "**ha sido un factor clave en el fomento de la confianza del consumidor hacia las compras en línea**," driven by the influence of cash and distrust of the online channel. Only **35.5% of Colombian adults have access to formal credit** (https://blog.envioclick.com/pago-contra-entrega-en-colombia-como-funciona-y-como-escalarlo-sin-perder-control/).

Rappi's own Colombian terms encode the choice: payment via the PAYMETEZ electronic system **or in cash on receipt of the products, at the Consumer's choice** (https://www.redjurista.com/appfolders/images/news/A_G_Rappi-04-04.pdf). Earlier reporting estimated **more than 60% of Rappi orders were paid in cash** (https://modelo-canvas.com/modelo-de-negocio-rappi/). Rappi Colombia now runs **8M+ orders/month with 1.4M monthly active users**, app opened 7M times weekly with ~35% of those users buying in a given week, and restaurants down from >80% of platform revenue three years ago to ~55% (https://www.larepublica.co/empresas/matias-laks-ceo-de-rappi-colombia-dijo-que-en-rappi-hoy-estamos-por-encima-de-las-ocho-millones-de-ordenes-por-mes-4177604).

Notably, Rappi's financial arm treats cash as a **feature, not a legacy**: RappiCuenta, backed by Davivienda, allows free cash withdrawal from Davivienda ATMs without a card (QR/code generated in-app) and **cash deposit via corresponsales** — the company's positioning is explicitly that "**7 de cada 10 transacciones en Colombia siguen siendo en efectivo**," and that no competing neobank lets you deposit physical cash (https://monopolombiano.com/economia-hoy/rappicuenta-2025-de-oveja-negra-a-la-opcion-mas-completa-del-ano).

- Brazilian ReMark 942-consumer study: trust in platform/product/community drives intention; trust in peers does NOT directly.
- Trust transfer theory: trust-in-platform → trust-in-seller → purchase intention (294 Taobao buyers); PEEIM (perceived effectiveness of e-commerce institutional mechanisms) NEGATIVELY moderates platform→seller trust, but POSITIVELY moderates seller→purchase intention. PWQS positively moderates platform→seller and negatively moderates seller→intention.
- Räisänen et al. systematic review: 45 articles; antecedents grouped by entity (seller, buyer, platform, interpersonal, transaction); "trust in this economy is often reduced to the use of reputation systems alone... trust is much more complex."
- Trust transfer between platforms study (jums.ub.uni-muenchen.de): imported ratings significantly affect perceived reputation of provider; trust in provider affected by overall trust in platform, perceived reputation, perceived social presence; evidence for trust transferability; validated ability/benevolence/integrity 3D scale.
- Peer-to-platform trust transfer (359 users): structural assurance, situational normality, payment security influence institutional trust; peer emotional/informational/instrumental support drive interpersonal trust; peer trust facilitates transfer to platforms.
- Platform-based mechanisms (PEPIS/PESEIM): PEPIS positively impacts trust in platform → continuous use; PESEIM negatively moderates PEPIS→trust and trust→continuous use.
- Institutional trust & repurchase: privacy concerns and security concerns moderate.
- Trust spillovers Airbnb (Utrecht): no evidence that prior Airbnb experience with a nationality increased trust in that nationality.
- Sharing economy index LATAM: "The region's digital lag, combined with generally low trust in government institutions and problems inherent to developing economies, such as low wages, and corruption, make it especially receptive to innovative solutions." Uber allowed cash payments and Uber Lite for those without credit cards/poor internet.

**Trust levels / informality:**
- Latinobarómetro 2023: Brazil interpersonal trust 3.9% ("one can trust most people"), 95.0% say "never too careful". Argentina 28±2.7, Colombia 17±2.4, Brazil 4±1.1 (2023, azenha dashboard). OWID 2022: Argentina 24.1%, Brazil 10.2%, Colombia 20.5% (Latinobarómetro); Argentina 17.4%, Brazil 9.2%, Colombia 14.3% (Integrated Values Survey).
- Latinobarómetro 2024: 19,214 face-to-face interviews, 17 countries; Latin America lowest interpersonal trust region in world (~15%).
- ILO: regional informal employment 47.6% mid-2024 (2023: 48%, 2019: 48.8%); Argentina informality 43.2%; 2022 regional 48.7%; 2019 50.6%, 2022 50.7%. Argentina includes only urban areas. Exceptions: Argentina, Brazil, Mexico had different patterns in 2024.
- Brazil: ~38% of economically active population in traditional informal sector (São Paulo, headreports).
- IADB Uber-IPSOS 2024: >13,000 Uber drivers in 8 countries (Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Dominican Republic, Argentina); drivers predominantly male, middle-aged, often part-time; majority in debt, using earnings for essentials; low social protection coverage.
- Nubank: Brazil 107.2M customers = 62% of adults; 31.5M opened first-ever bank account (nearly 1 in 5 Brazilian adults); leading "main bank" in every region; 80-90% of customers acquired organically via word-of-mouth/referral (older figure). Colombia: 5M customers ≈15% of adult population, ~1M got first credit card, in a country where ~65% had no formal credit access; COP$473bn (~US$130M) investment in 2026.
- Fairwork Argentina 2025: 7 platforms (PedidosYa, Rappi, Uber, Cabify, DiDi, Zolvers, QxM); context of high informality, purchasing-power loss, inflation, multi-job holding; "opaque algorithmic decision-making, sudden suspensions without meaningful appeal mechanisms"; "autonomy frequently constrained by rankings, performance metrics, economic incentives, and digital reputation systems."
- Fairwork Brazil 2025: workers charged when orders lost (accidents/theft) generating debt; vehicle rental debt.
- Fairwork Argentina 2022: scores 0-4; DiDi 4, only platform with any points.

**Deactivation/appeals interfaces:**
- Uber Brazil: Review Request Portal; 4 categories (criminal record → iAudit/Emptor portal; fraud; safety; low rating); 90 days; one request per case; at least one completed trip in Brazil; agent reviews within max 3 calendar days (global page); can submit video/audio evidence.
- Uber identity verification: selfie every 14 days for deliveries; Microsoft facial verification; faceprint; flagged photos → human review by three specialists; need 2+ to fail.
- iFood: contestation via app "esclarecer o que aconteceu"; documents + liveness proof; response within 2 business days; only deactivations within 90 days; account deletion doesn't reverse deactivation. Blocking categories (battery <15%, wrong time, unregistered phone, GPS off, pending facial recognition, etc.); blocks last 2h–48h (or up to 20 days per best-practices manual); desativação = definitive.
- iFood facial recognition used on: new device access, profile data changes, security requests by courier.
- G1: 22ª Vara do Trabalho de Brasília ordered iFood to pay R$60,000 moral damages to courier Tiago Alves after facial recognition failure; iFood denies racial analysis; appeal pending.
- Reclame Aqui complaints about iFood facial recognition failures blocking couriers.

Now, quantitative work I can show: computable ratios.

Let me compute a few things:
- Colombia COD 12% vs Argentina 4% = 3× higher.
- Colombia COD 12% vs Chile 2% = 6×.
- Pix 64 billion transactions 2024; Brazil adult population ~160M (gov.br 160M+ accounts). 64e9/160e6 ≈ 400 transactions per adult per year → ~33/month. Actually I should be careful. Let me use the Nubank figure of ~62% of adults = 107.2M customers, implying adult population ≈ 173M. Hmm, 107.2/0.62 = 172.9M adults. So 64e9/172.9e6 ≈ 370 Pix transactions per adult per year ≈ 31/month. That's a legit derived figure with stated assumptions.
- Argentina: 28.3 electronic payments per adult per month (Dec-24) vs 2.7 cash withdrawals — ratio ~10.5:1. That's from BCRA directly (13.1, 19.5, 28.3 appear to be a series or tiers — actually the table shows three columns maybe 2022/2023/2024; +45% YoY consistent with 19.5→28.3 = +45.1%. Yes! 19.5 × 1.451 = 28.3. Confirms. So 2023 = 19.5, 2024 = 28.3.)
- Argentina Sept 2024: MPE 95.3% of total vs cash 4.7% — but that's by amount, and note the caveat.
- Reclame Aqui: 108,762 COPREC claims 2024 with 28% resolved = ~30,453 resolved. Cost AR$650M/30,453 ≈ AR$21,345 per resolved claim. I can show that.
- Brazil interpersonal trust 3.9% vs Argentina 28% ≈ 7× gap (2023); vs Colombia 17% ≈ 4.4×.
- Colombia 65% without formal credit vs Argentina's wallet penetration 75%.

Let me be careful with the Latinobarómetro numbers: the azenha dashboard gives 2023 values: Mexico 31, Argentina 28, Colombia 17, Brazil 4, region 16. And Latinobarómetro 2023 Brazil country file gives 3.9% "one can trust most people" and 95.0% "never too careful". These agree.

OWID 2022: Argentina 24.1%, Brazil 10.2%, Colombia 20.5% (ESS/Latinobarómetro/Afrobarometer column); and 17.4%, 9.2%, 14.3% (Integrated Values Survey). Note the discrepancy in Brazil (10.2% vs 4%) — worth flagging as measurement sensitivity. Good, I should state uncertainty.

Now, structure the report:

1. Executive summary / headline findings
2. Method and evidence limits
3. Market context: informality + trust baseline (with the numbers)
4. Mechanism 1: Rating & reputation systems
5. Mechanism 2: Identity verification
6. Mechanism 3: Payment escrow & settlement
7. Mechanism 4: Dispute resolution interfaces
8. How prior trust-system experience affects adoption (trust transfer)
9. Country-by-country design implications (Argentina, Brazil, Colombia)
10. Cross-cutting design recommendations
11. What the evidence does NOT support / open questions
12. Source list

Actually the task asks for a report. Let me write it well-structured with clear country differentiation. I should be honest that some evidence is thin — e.g., no direct experimental evidence on "prior experiences with trust systems" specifically in these three markets; I have proxies.

Let me be careful about the trust-transfer literature: almost all of it is China/e-commerce, not LatAm. The Brazilian ReMark study is the most directly relevant (942 Brazilian consumers). That's a key finding: trust in peers does NOT directly affect intention to use in Brazil — which cuts against the standard peer-reputation-heavy design.

Important caveat: the ReMark study appeared with a 2026 date in search results; I'll cite it as such without over-claiming.

Let me also note the Correa et al. finding that the trust-sales relationship was "statistically inconsistent across nations" — meaning you can't assume one reputation design transfers across borders even within the same platform (Mercado Libre operates in 18 countries). That's a headline for a UX director.

Let me now write. I'll aim for a thorough but readable report. Use headers, inline URLs.

One more: the Mercado Livre reputation API shows "real_level": "red" alongside "level_id": "5_green" and "power_seller_status": "platinum" with "excluded" real values — this is evidence that platform reputation displays can diverge from underlying metrics, i.e., the displayed reputation is a managed/policy artifact. Good detail for a UX director about opacity.

Let me also do the escrow timing math: Mercado Pago release: 2 days (good reputation + Mercado Envios) vs up to 28 days (new/self-shipped) vs ~7 days automatic ML default (Bling). 28/2 = 14× difference in cash cycle based on reputation. That's a huge economic lever — reputation is literally working capital.

Also: Seller Protection requires ≥10 completed sales — an entry barrier that the informal seller may not clear.

Let me write the report now. I'll keep quantitative work explicit.

Length: this is a meaty research task; I'll write a comprehensive report but avoid padding. Maybe 2,500–3,500 words.

I need to make sure I don't include tool-call syntax or narration. Just the report.

Let me draft.

For citations, I'll use the URLs inline in parentheses.

Note on date discrepancy: some sources show 2026 dates (search index artifacts). I'll cite them as found.

Let me write.

# DSM-5 (2013) vs. ICD-11 (2019) Autism Diagnosis: Criteria, Evidence, Guidelines, Advocacy, Safety, and Coding

**Scope note and upfront caveat:** This report is grounded in the sources retrieved during research. One important finding must be stated plainly before anything else: **there is very little head-to-head empirical evidence comparing DSM-5 and ICD-11 autism criteria on diagnostic accuracy.** First et al. (2021) state explicitly that "there has been only a small number of studies comparing the ICD-11 CDDG and DSM-5 criteria for a particular disorder in terms of whether they are identifying the same people or yield similar prevalence estimates" (https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/3/Brewin_First%20et%20al%20ICD-11%20DSM-5%20differences%20World%20Psychiatry%20final%20accepted%20version.pdf). Several sections below therefore rely on ICD-10-vs-DSM-5 evidence as a proxy and on documentary/consensus sources, and I flag this wherever it occurs. Section D (advocacy organizations) is the weakest-evidenced section and I say so directly.

---

## (A) Side-by-side criteria table

Sources: ICD-11 6A02 text (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html; https://www.icd11-code.com/6a02/; https://www.findacode.com/icd-11/block-437815624.html; https://www.iccpp.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/ICD-11.pdf); WHO CDDR (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240077263); First et al. 2021 (https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/...); DSM-5 criteria as reproduced by AAP (https://www.maineaap.org/assets/resources/Autism-Clinical-Report.pdf) and the ICD-11 psychological review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/).

| Row | DSM-5 (2013 / DSM-5-TR 2022) | ICD-11 (2019 / CDDR 2024) |
|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | Criterion A requires **all three** of: A1 deficits in social-emotional reciprocity; A2 deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviours; A3 deficits in developing, maintaining and understanding relationships. Prescriptive and count-based. | "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication." No mandatory sub-criteria. Text states "manifestations **may include** the following" across ~7 listed areas (the First et al. 2021 analysis counts 19 described manifestations); social-communication examples map onto the three DSM-5 A-criteria. Non-prescriptive, concept-based. |
| **Sensory processing mention / weighting** | Listed as **B4** — one of four possible RRB sub-criteria: "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment." Threshold is **2 of 4** RRB sub-criteria, so sensory is an **optional, non-required** feature; it cannot alone support diagnosis. | Explicitly folded into the second essential domain: "restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities," whose examples include **hyper- and hypo-sensitivity/reactivity to sensory stimuli**. Like DSM-5, **not a required element** — ICD-11 mandates no minimum symptom count at all (SpringerMedizin: https://www.springermedizin.de/the-reclassification-of-neurodevelopmental-disorders-in-icd-11/51520996). The psychological review notes this inclusion is an **advance over ICD-10**, where sensory processing was not a diagnostic feature (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/). |
| **Weighting summary** | Sensory = 1 of 4 RRB options; can be "counted" toward the 2-of-4 threshold. ICD-11 = one of many illustrative RRB examples with no counting. **Net: neither manual makes sensory a required core criterion, and neither weights it more heavily in an operational sense, but ICD-11's exemplar set is broader and not ID-weighted** (First et al. 2021, above). |
| **Severity specifiers** | Explicit **Level 1 / 2 / 3** ("requiring support" → "requiring very substantial support") for **each** of the two domains, plus specifiers (with/without intellectual impairment, language impairment, known genetic/medical/environmental factor, associated neurodevelopmental/mental/behavioural disorder, catatonia). | **No operationalised severity levels.** Severity is captured via co-occurring axes: co-occurring **disorder of intellectual development** and **impairment of functional language**, yielding subtypes 6A02.0–6A02.5 (e.g., 6A02.0 = without DID, mild/no functional language impairment; 6A02.5 = with DID and absence of functional language). |
| **Age / onset requirements** | Symptoms present in the **early developmental period**; may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies. No rigid onset cut-off. | Onset **during the developmental period, typically early childhood**, but symptoms "may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." ICD-11 explicitly recognises **compensation/masking** and that presentation may occur in adolescence or adulthood (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/). |
| **Functional impairment threshold** | Required: "Symptoms cause **clinically significant impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." | Required: deficits "are **sufficiently severe to cause impairment** in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning," usually pervasive across settings though context-variable. |
| **Co-occurring conditions** | Historically prohibits some combinations (e.g., ADHD was excluded pre-DSM-5); requires specifiers. | Explicitly permits **ASD + ADHD coexistence** (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10411432/). |

---

## (B) Evidence synthesis: studies comparing DSM-5 vs. ICD-11

**State of the evidence.** No true diagnostic-accuracy head-to-head trial of DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 autism criteria was located. The best available sources are: (1) expert-consensus classification comparisons, (2) systematic review/meta-analysis of ICD-11 CDDR accuracy across disorders, and (3) primary studies using ICD-10-vs-DSM-5 as the closest proxy, plus one primary ICD-11 clinical-utility study involving ASD. GRADE ratings are **not reported in any source**; the ratings below are my own transparent assessments based on design, and are labelled as such.

**1. First et al., 2021 — expert-consensus classification comparison** (World Psychiatry 20:34–51; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825; accepted version https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/3/...).
- **Design:** Structured expert consensus (two principal raters) comparing ICD-11 CDDG essential features against DSM-5 criteria sets for 104 shared disorders.
- **Sample:** 104 diagnostic entities; ASD analysed qualitatively.
- **Key statistics:** Across all disorders — 20 (19.2%) rated "major difference," 42 (40.4%) "minor definitional difference," 10 (9.6%) "minor difference due to greater specification in DSM-5," 31 (29.8%) "essentially identical." For ASD specifically, the paper characterises the two systems as sharing a two-domain conceptual core but differing operationally: DSM-5 mandates all three social sub-criteria, ICD-11 does not; ICD-11 lists more non-ID exemplars. **The authors explicitly caution these ratings were "not based on empirical evidence"** because so few DSM-5-vs-ICD-11 head-to-head studies exist.
- **My GRADE-style rating:** **Very low** (expert opinion, not empirical diagnostic accuracy).

**2. Comparative accuracy of the ICD-11 CDDR — systematic review and meta-analysis of case-controlled field studies (2025)** (https://fair.unifg.it/handle/11369/472435).
- **Design:** Systematic review + random-effects meta-analysis of case-controlled field studies of the ICD-11 CDDR.
- **Sample:** 10 included studies; **264 effect sizes**.
- **Key statistics:** ICD-11 CDDR clinical-judgment accuracy **significantly higher than ICD-10 CDDG** (Q = 17.35 (1), p < 0.0001); slight, non-significant superiority for mood disorders; all guidelines performed poorly for subclinical conditions.
- **Caveat:** Results are for mental/behavioural disorders broadly; **ASD-specific effect sizes are not reported in the retrieved material.**
- **My GRADE-style rating:** **Low** (systematic review/meta-analysis of field studies, but indirect population; heterogeneity and non-ASD-specific).

**3. Gaebel et al., 2020 — web-based field study** (European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience 270(3); https://epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/78868/).
- **Design:** Web-based vignette field study of diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility, ICD-11 CDDG vs. ICD-10 CDDG.
- **Sample:** **928 health professionals** across all WHO regions; 10 disorders.
- **Key statistics:** Overall diagnostic accuracy **71.9% (ICD-11) vs. 53.2% (ICD-10)**; advantages largely limited to new ICD-11 diagnoses; ICD-11 never inferior; accuracy consistent across WHO regions and independent of clinical experience.
- **Caveat:** ASD was **not one of the 10 disorders** studied — **indirect evidence only.**
- **My GRADE-style rating:** **Low** (large international study; indirect to ASD).

**4. ICD-11 field-trial reliability study (Reed et al., 2018)** (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5980511/).
- **Design:** Clinic-based concurrent joint-rater reliability study of ICD-11 diagnostic guidelines.
- **Sample:** **1,806 patients**, 339 clinicians, 28 centres, 13 countries.
- **Key statistics:** Intraclass kappa **0.45 (dysthymic disorder) to 0.88 (social anxiety disorder)** — moderate to almost perfect; ICD-11 reliability superior to comparable ICD-10 data.
- **Caveat:** Covered high-burden adult disorders (psychotic, mood, anxiety, stress) — **no ASD-specific reliability estimate.**
- **My GRADE-style rating:** **Low–moderate** (large, multi-country, but indirect population).

**5. Lemay et al., 2024 — primary empirical clinical-utility study involving ASD** (Journal of Intellectual Disability Research; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38733333/).
- **Design:** International multi-site implementation/clinical-utility study of ICD-11 behavioural indicators (BIs), including co-occurring ASD.
- **Sample:** **116 children/adolescents (5–18 y)** across four sites — Italy (n=18), Sri Lanka (n=19), two India sites (n=79).
- **Key statistics:** BIs classified a higher proportion as **mild** severity vs. standardised measures (which skewed severe); individuals with **co-occurring ASD had more severe impairments** on both BIs and standardised measures; BIs rated clinically useful but required **more time/consideration when ASD and DID co-occurred.** Related earlier study (n=206) reported BI inter-rater reliability **ICC 0.91–0.97** and concurrent validity **ICC 0.66–0.82** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35170825/).
- **Caveat:** Evaluates ICD-11 DID severity indicators with ASD as a co-occurring condition — **not a DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 ASD head-to-head.**
- **My GRADE-style rating:** **Low–moderate** (prospective multi-site primary study; indirect to the exact question).

**Supporting primary empirical studies (ICD-10/DSM-IV vs. DSM-5 — proxy evidence for the direction of effect):**
- **Huerta et al., 2012** — n=977 (657 ASD clinical diagnoses). DSM-5 sensitivity **60.6%** (95% CI 57–64%); specificity **94.9%** (95% CI 92–97%); sensitivity varied by subgroup (Autistic Disorder .76; Asperger's .25; PDD-NOS .28) and IQ (<70 = .70; ≥70 = .46). (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/)
- **Frazier et al.** — n=14,744 siblings (8,911 ASD). DSM-5 specificity **.97 vs. .86** (DSM-IV-TR), but sensitivity **.81 vs. .95**; relaxing DSM-5 by one symptom raised sensitivity to **.93** with specificity **.95**. (https://cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/h702qd81k)
- **Wilson et al., 2013** — n=150 intellectually able adults. Of those with an ICD-10R ASD diagnosis, only **56%** met DSM-5 ASD criteria; a further **19%** met draft Social Communication Disorder; **78%** of DSM-IV-TR autistic/Asperger cases met DSM-5 ASD. (https://studyres.com/doc/8611005/...)
- **Singapore study (McDonnell et al.)** — n=110 children. DSM-IV-TR sensitivity **0.946**/specificity **0.889** vs. DSM-5 sensitivity **0.837**/specificity **0.833**; 40% of PDD-NOS best-estimate cases misclassified on DSM-5. (https://www.academia.edu/105867192/...)
- **Spanish child/adolescent study (2021)** — DSM-5 sensitivity ranged **.69–1.00** (higher in females), specificity **.64–.73**; 83.3% of autism-disorder cases retained an ASD diagnosis. (https://www.elsevier.es/en-revista-revista-psiquiatria-salud-mental-486-articulo-sensitivity-specificity-dsm-5-diagnostic-criteria-S2173505021000509)

**Quantitative illustration of the sensitivity/specificity trade-off (Frazier et al.):** DSM-5 sensitivity .81 vs. DSM-IV-TR .95 on 8,911 ASD cases implies roughly 8,911 × (0.95 − 0.81) ≈ **1,248 additional ASD children not meeting DSM-5 criteria** in that cohort, offset by a false-positive reduction of the same cohort size × (0.97 − 0.86) ≈ **980 fewer false positives**. This is the empirical backbone of the "DSM-5 trades sensitivity for specificity" narrative that is commonly assumed — but not yet demonstrated — to apply to ICD-11.

**Direction of likely ICD-11 effect:** The German ICD-10→ICD-11 review (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33269947/) predicts that because ICD-11 closely mirrors DSM-5 and drops "atypical autism," **prevalence may slightly decrease relative to ICD-10, sensitivity should remain high, and specificity may increase** — an explicit prediction, not measured.

---

## (C) Clinical guideline positions (WHO, APA, AAP, NICE)

- **WHO.** ICD-11 is WHO's own classification; the 2024 **Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements (CDDR)** are the operational clinical manual (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240077263; https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content). WHO's stated design goals are **clinical utility and global applicability alongside validity**, with a deliberately less prescriptive, non-count-based format. Sensory processing is incorporated within the second essential domain. WHO does **not** publish a separate clinical guideline on which manual to use — ICD-11 *is* its instrument.
- **APA.** The APA publishes DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022) and has not adopted ICD-11 autism criteria. DSM-5 retains prescriptive counts (all 3 social; 2 of 4 RRB), explicit Level 1–3 severity, and sensory as the optional B4. The DSM-5-TR vs. ICD-11 comparison in the retrieved differential-diagnosis review notes "substantial overlap, but not complete alignment" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/).
- **American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).** The 2020 AAP clinical report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" (Hyman et al.) is built around **DSM-5** criteria and recommends universal screening at 18 and 24 months plus ongoing surveillance. Its autism toolkit explicitly includes a "DSM-5 ASD Criteria With Examples" item and a "Relationship Between DSM-5 and ICD-10-CM" item, but **no ICD-11 adoption** (https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit; https://composer.publications.aap.org/media/qs5dwvua/2020-april-asd-webinar.pdf; clinical report text: https://www.maineaap.org/assets/resources/Autism-Clinical-Report.pdf). **Sensory weighting:** AAP lists "hyper/hypo-reactivity to sensory input" as criterion B4 of four (2 required), i.e., it mirrors DSM-5's optional weighting.
- **NICE (UK).** NICE CG128 states autism is diagnosed if behaviours "meet the criteria defined in the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-11) and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition (DSM-5)" (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Context). **Crucially, NICE updated its guidance in March 2022 to change mentions of ICD-10 to ICD-11, "which the NHS adopted in March 2022"** (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information). NICE QS51 requires the diagnostic assessment to cover "repetitive and stereotyped behaviours, **including sensory sensitivities**," and the strengths/needs profile must include "**sensory sensitivities**" (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs51/chapter/Quality-statement-1-Diagnostic-assessment-by-an-autism-team). So NICE formally accommodates ICD-11 and treats sensory profile as an assessed domain of need — but not as a diagnostic threshold criterion. NICE also cautions that some children have features that "do not reach the ICD-10 or DSM-5 diagnostic criteria" (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553265/).

**Summary of guideline positions:** WHO = ICD-11 is the system. APA = DSM-5/DSM-5-TR. AAP = DSM-5 adopted, ICD-11 not referenced for diagnosis. NICE = accepts both, and the NHS operationally migrated to ICD-11 in March 2022.

---

## (D) Advocacy-organisation positions

**This section carries a major evidence limitation, stated candidly: I did not retrieve any primary or peer-reviewed source documenting stated positions of the Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN), the National Autistic Society (NAS), or Autism Speaks specifically comparing DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 criteria on neurodiversity-affirming grounds, nor any of them citing sensory-processing weighting.** I will not manufacture citations. What the retrieved evidence *does* support:

- **The neurodiversity framing exists in the peer-reviewed literature, not (in the sources I found) attributed to these organisations.** The ICD-11 psychological review (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/) discusses the biopsychosocial/neurodiversity model — citing Bolis et al. 2017, Greaves-Lord et al. 2022 and Mandy 2022 — in which autistic difficulty is framed as a "poor fit" between the individual and environmental demands, and autistic "symptoms" are seen as neurodiversity. It notes the ICD-11 "endorses a medical model" even while acknowledging a rising stakeholder preference for a biopsychosocial alternative.
- **The structural features most commonly cited as neurodiversity-relevant do differ between the manuals:** ICD-11 (a) recognises masking/compensation and adult presentation, (b) does not force count-based thresholds, and (c) does not weight exemplars toward intellectual-disability-associated behaviours (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/; https://www.springermedizin.de/the-reclassification-of-neurodevelopmental-disorders-in-icd-11/51520996). These are the features a neurodiversity-affirming position would plausibly favour — but the sources do **not** contain an advocacy organisation saying so.
- **NICE's terminology shift** — June 2021 changes from "children and young people with autism" to "autistic children and young people," and "symptoms" to "features" to align with current terminology — is the closest documented institutional move toward identity-first/neurodiversity-aligned language (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information), but it is a guideline body, not an advocacy organisation, and it applies to both manuals.

**Bottom line for (D):** On the evidence actually retrieved, I **cannot** rank DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 as "more neurodiversity-affirming" on the basis of any ASAN, NAS, or Autism Speaks citation. Any statement that one manual is more affirming on the basis of these three organisations' stated positions would be unsupported here. This should be treated as an open evidence gap requiring direct primary retrieval of ASAN/NAS/Autism Speaks position statements.

---

## (E) Diagnostic safety risks (misdiagnosis, over-/under-diagnosis, inappropriate interventions)

**Over-diagnosis / false-positive risk (ICD-11 specifically).** The strongest, most direct safety argument in the retrieved literature is the perspective article "Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11—a critical reflection of its possible impact on clinical practice and research" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). It argues ICD-11's high variety of permissible symptom combinations, absence of mandatory social-communication features, and vague/subjective concepts risk **false-positive diagnoses**, **further increased prevalence rates**, **limitations of access to ASD-specific services** (through dilution/rationing), **increasing non-specificity of treatments**, reduced specificity versus other mental disorders/autism-like traits, and hampered replicability. It characterises the direction of travel as moving "from an observable, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorder to a disorder of inner experience that can hardly be measured objectively." This is a **perspective/theoretical critique**, not an empirical incidence estimate — a critical distinction.

**Under-diagnosis / false-negative risk (DSM-5 specifically).** The empirical record shows DSM-5's higher specificity costs sensitivity, especially in non-ID/Asperger-type presentations:
- Huerta et al.: DSM-5 sensitivity 60.6%; Asperger's subgroup sensitivity only **.25** (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/).
- Wilson et al.: only **56%** of ICD-10R-diagnosed adults met DSM-5 ASD criteria — with the authors warning "some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services" (https://studyres.com/doc/8611005/...).
- Singapore: 40% of PDD-NOS cases misclassified (https://www.academia.edu/105867192/...).
- DSM-5 sensitivity was also lower for the "low-functioning" IQ category in the Spanish study (https://www.elsevier.es/en-revista-revista-psiquiatria-salud-mental-486-articulo-sensitivity-specificity-dsm-5-diagnostic-criteria-S2173505021000509).

**Sensory-focused presentations specifically.** No retrieved source provides direct evidence that DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 differences produce misdiagnosis in *sensory-focused* presentations. The indirect logic is: in **both** manuals sensory features are non-required (DSM-5: 1 of 4 RRB options, 2 required; ICD-11: illustrative example, no required count). Therefore a genuinely sensory-predominant presentation **without** social-communication and other RRB features cannot reach the diagnostic threshold under either manual. The safety implication, flagged but not quantified in the sources: such individuals fall into "sub-threshold"/unspecified categories — DSM-5's "other specified/unspecified neurodevelopmental disorder," or ICD-11's **6E60 secondary neurodevelopmental syndrome** which the differential-diagnosis review notes is used when a person "meets some but not all criteria for ASD" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/). NICE likewise notes features that "do not reach the ICD-10 or DSM-5 diagnostic criteria" and advises referral to appropriate services without a definitive autism diagnosis (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553265/).

**Intervention/provision risk.** Two sources raise service-access risk, in opposite directions: the ICD-11 critique warns that ICD-11 over-inclusiveness may limit access to ASD-specific services (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/), while the ICD-10→ICD-11 review predicts prevalence consolidation/slight decrease (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33269947/) — and the Wilson et al. findings document that a criteria tightening already produced an access threat under DSM-5 (https://studyres.com/doc/8611005/...). No source quantifies actual intervention harm from either manual.

**Severity/classification risk (ICD-11).** Lemay et al. found ICD-11 behavioural indicators skew toward **mild** severity relative to standardised measures and require **extra time/caution** when ASD and intellectual disability co-occur (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146) — a potential under-recognition of severity risk specific to ICD-11.

**Residual uncertainty:** All (E) findings are either theoretical critique, ICD-10/DSM proxy studies, or specific to DID-with-ASD. Direct measured rates of DSM-5-vs-ICD-11 misdiagnosis in autism were not found.

---

## (F) Reimbursement / coding summary

**United States.**
- The HIPAA-mandated US code set is **ICD-10-CM** (adopted Oct 2015), not ICD-11. ASD maps to the F84 block: **F84.0 autistic disorder**, F84.5 Asperger's syndrome, F84.8, **F84.9 pervasive developmental disorder, unspecified** (crosswalk table at https://a4.org.au/book/export/html/4). The DSM-5→ICD-10-CM relationship is explicitly addressed in AAP's autism toolkit as "Relationship Between DSM-5 and ICD-10-CM" (https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit).
- **ICD-11 has not been adopted for US morbidity coding.** Therefore ICD-11 criteria adoption has **no current effect on US coverage or reimbursement** on the evidence retrieved; US payers still code via ICD-10-CM (which derives from ICD-10, whose autism subtypes — including the "atypical autism" category ICD-11 drops — still exist in the US code set). DSM-5 is the diagnostic criteria set that US clinicians and payers actually apply.

**European Union / UK.**
- WHO **ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics (MMS)** is the global standard, and **NICE records that "the NHS adopted [ICD-11] in March 2022"** (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information). This is the clearest documented payer/system-level mapping shift in the retrieved sources: UK clinical coding migrated from ICD-10 to ICD-11.
- ICD-11 autism coding uses **6A02** with subtypes 6A02.0–6A02.5 (intellectual development and functional language axes) rather than DSM-5 severity Levels 1–3 and rather than ICD-10's F84.0/F84.1/F84.5. Practically, this means **different granularity** in reimbursement-relevant coding, though the retrieved sources do not quantify any resulting change in payment.

**Does ICD-11 adoption change coverage/reimbursement?** On the retrieved evidence: **No direct evidence of a quantified coverage or reimbursement effect was found for either the US or the EU.** The only relevant signals are indirect: (i) the UK NHS/ICD-11 coding migration (above); (ii) the ICD-11 critique's concern about "limitations of access to ASD-specific services" as a hypothetical consequence (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/); and (iii) the ICD-10→ICD-11 review's prediction of slightly reduced prevalence as "atypical autism" disappears (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33269947/), which, if realised, could narrow the population eligible for autism-linked services and benefits. These are **predictions and concerns, not measured payer outcomes**, and should not be presented as established reimbursement findings.

---

**Key bottom line for the sensory-weighting question specifically:** neither DSM-5 nor ICD-11 makes sensory processing a *required* diagnostic criterion, and neither weights it more heavily than the other in an operational sense. The meaningful differences are that (a) ICD-11 explicitly recognises sensory reactivity within its second essential domain and, unlike ICD-10, counts it as a diagnostic feature at all; (b) ICD-11 requires no minimum symptom count, so a sensory feature is one of many optional illustrations rather than a countable "B4"; and (c) ICD-11 recognises masking/compensation and later-life manifestation that DSM-5 mentions but operationalises more narrowly. Neither manual supports a sensory-only diagnosis, and no retrieved source quantifies the diagnostic or reimbursement consequence of that shared limitation.
